stories.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.titleZh: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.author: jaz
summaryZh: watch nowNvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO, effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk." President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.Shares of Nvidia closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6."I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia stock chart.Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said. Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations. Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.""On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote. Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX, Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.Read more Nvidia newsHuang reinstatement reignites voter angst over tech's outsized powerJensen Huang's Nvidia return highlights U.S.-China AI talent raceNvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh's push to read market signals: LiesmanAI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeezeJensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession planTrump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in WashingtonAG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigationCongress blasts Nvidia bringing Jensen Huang backJensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTCFor weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it.""The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China. Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips."The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement Monday. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls.""Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huangwatch now

comments.author: icyfox
comments.textZhHtml:
Some takes (and from talking to nvidia people):

- Delaware precedent in Caremark has a very high bar for culpability of boards in matters like this. So I suspect the combination of DoJ saying they won't prosecute combined with this standard will successfully remove their individual liability.

- I'm surprised this decision was completely unanimous at the board level, considering how they quickly forced him out. Full 180 in under two weeks.

- The news media is really confusing selling chips to Megaspeed then hosting them in Malaysia (giving chinese companies access - afaik still legal under the old export regime) and Megaspeed smuggling these physical chips for hosting in Chinese data centers. Former was legal and second was not.

- I would not be surprised if a pardon was mentioned at some point. Will be watching how state AGs end up getting involved. CA has already subpoenaed Nvidia for this.

- There was a drum circle at Nvidia from employees who were petitioning to get him back

Disclosure: I co-host a podcast that talks about this. More discussion if anyone is interested: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8nLiELIhwA

stories.titleZh: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
stories.author: Kotlopou
summaryZh: I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.

Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP—hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4—a lower bound (!!), matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.

comments.author: nickysielicki
comments.textZhHtml:
I have no real confidence in this take, but I’ll go against the grain and argue that the labs do not presently have cracks in cryptosystems. I believe they’re working on it, and it’s good that they are, but I don’t think there’s evidence right now that they have fundamental breakthroughs in cryptography.

For one, the labs are now massive. I don’t think you can keep a secret like this under wraps for long in an office. I think we would be seeing whistleblowers or leakers. It’s too big.

Secondly, the people working at labs know that anything a frontier model can do can be approximated by the models available to the public given 10x the tokens and 10x the time and a little bit of informed direction. So they would know it’s only a matter of time before someone in the public discovers the same flaws and potentially uses it for evil. If they were sitting on this, they would try to minimize the damage and would try to warn the public to start moving to more secure encryption schemes because they know there’s a ticking time bomb until its public anyway. But they’re not doing that.

That’s not to say that it won’t happen in the next few weeks. I just don’t think it’s happened yet.

Edit: Alternatively, not to contradict myself, if they discovered this and immediately went to the US government (likely), and the US government served them a gag order (also likely), then this would look the exact same. Who knows.

We also have little info on how much compute they spent to achieve their results. Therefore, it’s hard to decouple the two. However, since the general math community seems to be relegated to doing verification as opposed to discovery despite being able to crowd source compute, that leads me to believe that the frontier labs really do have a special sauce.

stories.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
stories.author: janvdberg
summaryZh: Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux. I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^) Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional. This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that. If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol. Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

comments.author: simscitizen

Browsers are runtimes and webpages are apps. They just happen to be apps that are dynamically fetched over the network and are packaged as HTML/CSS/JS instead of as PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries.

Runtimes can have bugs or inefficiencies that cause them to use more memory than strictly necessary, but by and large most memory problems are the product of the apps (or webpages) themselves.

comments.author: panta
comments.textZhHtml: The view of web pages as apps and browsers as runtime environments/OSes is reasonable but in my opinion it even reinforces the idea that it should be the browser duty to contain bad behavior from web apps/pages. Browsers are well positioned to do so, as they know exactly which resources are used by each tab , and how those grow over time. Also browsers already treat web content as untrusted (sandboxing, isolation), so it would be a natural next step to extend that approach to resource usage. It would match how Operating Systems work, where it's the OS acting as an "arbiter", not the userland application.

stories.title: 1Password Security Incident
stories.author: lxhrstn
summaryZh: Update: We will be providing a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) with details in the coming weeks once our full investigation is complete.What happenedOn November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.What information was affectedThe attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:Names and email addressesAccount and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in timesPublic keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account) Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recoveryOther non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security. comments.author: tptacek
comments.textZhHtml:
This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.

In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.

Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.

So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack.

I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

stories.author: rmason
summaryZh: Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Emma Roth

Pangram (AI writing detector) is a lot more accurate than people think it is, but it measures something very different than what people think it measures.

Let's say two groups of people are writing scientific papers. The first is a group of native speakers of English who don't actually do any research, generate the paper from scratch, but then rewrite everything in their own words. They'll get a 0% (meaning human written) on Pangram.

Let's say the other group consists of non-native speakers of English who understand the language well, but are bad at writing in a style suitable for publication in a journal, so they write every paragraph in their own language and have AI translate. They've done all the research, they've had human authors understand and accept every single word of the paper, yet Pangram will tell them that the paper has been written by AI.

comments.textZhHtml:
For the general picture: the Xbox version of the game was leaked by Cyberleek - first the resources, then the game binary.

Because modern Xbox is very close to a Windows PC with some extra Xbox stuff, running the actual game code isn't hard, it's mostly about compatibility and graphics, plus the binary doesn't have any special DRM/obfuscation.

The current projects (xcl and VIctory) basically take a Wine-like approach. The main problems they have to solve, as I understand:

- The game ships with raw RDNA 2 shaders, so the projects have to translate that to another format, e.g. DXIL for DirectX 12, and compile those shaders. So you need a good translation/recompilation pipeline, if it's bad, the shaders will be bloated and perform poorly

- Xbox has unified memory, while most PCs do not, so you have to add a lot of workarounds and book-keeping for the game to work properly with that

- Xbox's DirectX 12 differs from the normal Windows one in some ways, and the game uses Xbox-specific texture formats with DirectStorage

I just wanted to share this because there's a lot of misconceptions going around about this being a "recomp" or something like that. Decompiling the entire binary (it's about 100MB of real executable machine code) will be a much bigger effort than getting this binary to run.

stories.title: AI made self-hosting fun again
stories.author: jlelse
summaryZh: I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

comments.author: DanielHB
comments.textZhHtml:
The problem with this kind of advice is that sometimes you just want to _relax_ instead of _engage_. Doomscrolling is a low-effort activity that can't (always) be replaced by a high mental effort activity.

The dangerous thing of doomscrolling is that it is very engaging both when you are in low-energy mode (exausted afterwork for example) and when you are in high-energy mode (just woken up in the morning). I argue that doomscrolling is not harmful if you are low energy. However because of its highly engaging nature, it bleeds into your high energy time too.

So, for example, listening to music is a better alternative to low-energy doomscrolling, while a book is a better alternative to high-energy doomscrolling.

Have you considered, i dunno, actually tackling those projects and challenges yourself instead of turning them into simple prompts? Do you remember how to do that? Or that doing so is even an option?

Yeah, it'll take longer, but that's the whole point. It's a lot easier to get bored when you instantly finish everything exciting than it is when spending a long time finishing one exciting thing.

When fighting boredom you're ultimately just trying to kill time in an enjoyable way. Taking a slow yet fun journey is far more effective than reaching your destination with the fastest, lowest effort route.
